442.title: Beha'alotcha: a second Passover (Numbers 9:6–14)
442.hook: people who missed Passover ask for a chance, and one is given
442.howItsDone: Pesach Sheni falls on the fourteenth of Iyar, a month after Passover; with no Temple offering today, some Jews mark it by eating some matzah, and some communities omit penitential prayers that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aaron held the light until it rose alone, and your line was until it rises alone. Did you stay with someone through a first try, then step back? Day four hundred forty-two.

A group of people walk up to Moses with a complaint that sounds almost like a lawsuit. Everyone else is getting ready to keep Passover in the wilderness, a year after leaving Egypt. The lambs are chosen. The fires are being built. And these people can't take part. It's not their fault. They're ritually impure, because they've been near a dead body. Somebody had to handle the dead. And they want to know: why should we be left out? What happens next is striking. Moses doesn't give them an answer. He says: wait, and I'll ask.
screen: `EVERYONE IS READY FOR PASSOVER.` → `A GROUP LEFT OUT.` → `MOSES SAYS: WAIT.`

segments.voice: Numbers nine. The men say: we're impure from a dead body, "wherefore are we to be kept back," from bringing the LORD's offering at its time with everyone else? Moses tells them to wait while he asks. This law doesn't start as a command from above. It starts from below: it starts with people who refuse to accept being shut out, and say so. God's answer creates a new date. Anyone impure from the dead, or far away on a journey, can keep Passover one month later, on the fourteenth of the second month, with matzah and bitter herbs. In Hebrew, Pesach Sheni: the second Passover. Who were they? The Talmud records a few opinions. One says they were the people carrying Joseph's coffin, the bones Moses brought out of Egypt. Another suggests they had buried someone who died with no one else to bury them. Either way, they were impure because they'd done something good. The Torah is honest about the edge of this, too. For someone who was clean, not on a journey, and simply didn't keep Passover, the verse has hard words: he shall bear his sin. The second date is written for people life got in the way of. Today, there's no Passover offering, but the date is still marked. Some Jews eat a piece of matzah on that day, a month after Passover. And in Chabad teaching it's often summed up with a simple line: it's never too late. The door you missed can open again.
screen: `WHEREFORE ARE WE KEPT BACK?` · `A LAW THAT STARTS FROM BELOW.` · `ONE MONTH LATER: PESACH SHENI.` · `FOR THOSE LIFE GOT IN THE WAY OF.` · then, large: `SECOND CHANCES EXIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone a second chance. Breathe, and think of someone who missed something with you: a birthday, a promise, a deadline, a moment you needed them. Ask whether life got in the way of them, the way it did for the people in the story. Hold that possibility gently. Then picture offering a second date: let's try again next week, I'd still like to hear about it, the door's open. You can also offer yourself one. The bell holds the time.
Pesach Sheni. The second Passover: one month later, for those who couldn't keep the first, given because they asked.
Your line: second chances exist. Today, offer one, to someone else or to yourself, with a real date on it. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BEHA'ALOTCHA: WE REMEMBER THE FISH (NUMBERS 11:4–6).`

443.title: Beha'alotcha: we remember the fish (Numbers 11:4–6)
443.hook: the people crave Egypt's fish and cucumbers, forgetting the whip
443.howItsDone: The people's craving for Egypt's food in Numbers 11 is read in Beha'alotcha each summer; Jewish teachers often use Rashi's reading of "for nought" to talk about how the memory of slavery can be softened into longing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesach Sheni, the second Passover, and your line, second chances exist. Did someone get one, maybe you? Day four hundred forty-three.

Someone runs into an ex at a party, and for one dangerous second remembers only the good parts. The road trip. The inside joke. The way they made coffee. Somehow the months of feeling small have gone blurry. Or it's an old job they hated, and now they catch themselves saying, the people were great, though. Memory is a generous editor. It keeps the flavor and cuts the cost. The Israelites, out of slavery and eating manna in the desert, do exactly this, and the Torah quotes their grocery list.
screen: `ONLY THE GOOD PARTS.` → `MEMORY, THE GENEROUS EDITOR.` → `A GROCERY LIST FROM EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Numbers eleven. The camp starts to crave. First the mixed crowd that came out of Egypt with them, then everyone, weeping in their tent doorways. They say: "We remember the fish, which we were wont to eat in Egypt for nought; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic". And now, they say, our throats are dry, and there's nothing but this manna. It's such a vivid list you can almost smell it. Leeks and onions and garlic. But look at two words: for nought. Free. The fish in Egypt were free? The rabbis didn't buy it. The Sifrei, and Rashi after it, ask: these were people who weren't even given straw for free to make their bricks. Who was handing them free fish? No, the rabbis say, here's what free really meant. Free of commandments. Free of responsibility. In Egypt, nobody asked anything of them except labor, and nobody expected them to choose. That's a kind of ease, and it's real. Freedom is heavier. And notice what the list leaves out completely. No whip. No quota of bricks. No baby boys thrown into the river. The craving doesn't lie about the cucumbers. It just forgets everything around them. The Torah doesn't mock them for missing food. Missing things is human. It just puts their own words on the record, so anyone reading later can hear what nostalgia does.
screen: `THE CAMP STARTS TO CRAVE.` · `FISH, MELONS, LEEKS, GARLIC.` · `FOR NOUGHT? FREE OF WHAT?` · `THE LIST LEAVES OUT THE WHIP.` · then, large: `EGYPT WASN'T FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice nostalgia for a bad place. Breathe, and let one old place come back to you: a job, a relationship, a city, a habit you quit. Notice the first memories that arrive. Probably the cucumbers. Then, gently, ask for the rest of the picture. What did it cost you to be there? What did you leave for a reason? You don't have to hate the place. Just hold the whole memory, flavor and cost together. The bell holds the time.
Beha'alotcha, the portion of the lamps, and of the night the people wept for Egypt's fish and forgot its whip.
Your line: Egypt wasn't free. Today, when you catch yourself missing something you left, finish the memory before you act on it. Day four hundred forty-three.

444.title: Beha'alotcha: seventy elders (Numbers 11:16–29)
444.hook: Moses shares the load and says "would that all the LORD's people were prophets"
444.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the seventy elders as a root of shared leadership, and the Mishnah links the great court of seventy-one, the Sanhedrin, to Moses and the seventy; Moses' answer to Joshua is often quoted as a model of a leader without jealousy.

segments.voice: Yesterday the people wept for Egypt's fish, and your line was Egypt wasn't free. Did you finish a memory before acting on it? Today, the same complaint, and what it does to Moses. Day four hundred forty-four.

Every office has one: the person who does everything. They answer every email, fix every crisis, and carry the whole project in their head, until one afternoon they sit in the car in the parking lot and can't make themselves go in. Moses hits that wall in Numbers eleven. A whole people is weeping for meat at their tent doors, and he turns to God and says something close to: did I give birth to these people? Am I supposed to carry them like a nurse carries a baby? I can't do this alone. It's too heavy for me.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES EVERYTHING.` → `I CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.` → `MOSES HITS THE WALL.`

segments.voice: God's answer isn't a pep talk. It's a reorganization. Gather seventy of the elders, God says. I'll take some of the spirit that is on you and put it on them, and they'll carry the burden of the people with you, so you don't carry it alone. Moses gathers them around the tent of meeting, and the spirit rests on them, and they prophesy. But two men named on the list, Eldad and Medad, stayed back in the camp. And the spirit rests on them there too. They start prophesying in the middle of the camp, outside the official circle. A young man runs to tell Moses. Joshua, Moses' loyal assistant, is alarmed: my lord Moses, stop them. Moses answers: are you jealous for my sake? "would that all the LORD'S people were prophets, that the LORD would put His spirit upon them!" Notice what Moses does twice. First, he shares the load: seventy people now carry what one was crushing under. Second, he shares the credit, and more than shares it. Two unauthorized prophets in the camp aren't a threat to him. He wishes everyone had what they have. Later Jewish tradition saw the beginnings of the great court here: seventy elders plus Moses, seventy-one, the number of the Sanhedrin. But the line that lasts is Moses' wish. A leader who wants everyone to have the spirit isn't diminished by it. He's freed.
screen: `TOO HEAVY FOR ME ALONE.` · `SEVENTY SHARE THE SPIRIT.` · `ELDAD AND MEDAD, IN THE CAMP.` · `ARE YOU JEALOUS FOR MY SAKE?` · then, large: `WOULD ALL WERE PROPHETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one burden and one credit. Breathe, and look at what you're carrying alone that someone else could hold a piece of: a chore, a worry, a project, a care for an aging parent. Name one person who could take a corner. Then look the other way: is there someone doing well, maybe outside the official circle, whose success you've been quietly guarding against? Picture saying out loud, good for you. I wish more of us could. The bell holds the time.
Beha'alotcha, the portion where Moses, overwhelmed, shares his spirit with seventy elders, and wishes it on everyone.
Your line: would all were prophets. Today, hand off one piece of a burden, and give away one piece of credit. Day four hundred forty-four.

445.title: Beha'alotcha: five words (Numbers 12:13)
445.hook: Moses' prayer for Miriam is five Hebrew words: heal her now, O God
445.howItsDone: Moses' five-word prayer, El na r'fa na lah, is often quoted in Jewish prayer for the sick, and synagogues recite the Mi Shebeirach for healing with the names of those who are ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday seventy elders shared Moses' load, and your line was would all were prophets. Did you hand off a burden, or give away some credit? Today, the last scene of this portion. Day four hundred forty-five.

A hospital waiting room at three in the morning. Nobody there is giving speeches. People mutter things like please, please, or just a name, over and over. A father in a plastic chair whispers four or five words into his folded hands and then says nothing for an hour. Ask anyone who's sat in that room whether those words counted. Moses once stood in exactly that kind of moment, for his own sister. His whole prayer was five words long.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PLEASE, PLEASE, A NAME.` → `FIVE WORDS FOR HIS SISTER.`

segments.voice: Numbers twelve. Miriam and Aaron speak against their brother Moses, about the Cushite woman he married, and about something deeper: has God spoken only through Moses? Hasn't God spoken through us too? The Torah pauses to say that Moses was very humble, more than anyone on earth. Then God calls all three out to the tent, defends Moses, and leaves. And Miriam is struck with a skin affliction, white as snow. Aaron turns to Moses and begs. And Moses, who has just been criticized by her, cries out: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee." In Hebrew: El na, r'fa na lah. Five words. No speech, no list of her merits, no bargaining. Just her, God, and now. The Talmud, in Berakhot, tells of a student leading prayer who went on and on, and the others complained. The teacher, Rabbi Eliezer, said: he's no longer than Moses, who prayed forty days and nights. Another time a student prayed very briefly, and they complained again. Rabbi Eliezer said: he's no shorter than Moses, who prayed El na, r'fa na lah. Both lengths count. Miriam is shut outside the camp for seven days. And the people don't move until she comes back. The Mishnah says why: once, Miriam waited by the river to watch over baby Moses. So a whole nation waited for her.
screen: `MIRIAM AND AARON SPEAK AGAINST MOSES.` · `EL NA, R'FA NA LAH.` · `TOO LONG? TOO SHORT? BOTH COUNT.` · `A NATION WAITS FOR MIRIAM.` · then, large: `SHORT PRAYERS COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in five words. Breathe, and bring to mind one person who's sick, hurting or struggling. See their face. If you pray, you can use Moses' own five words, heal her now, O God, or heal him, and say them slowly, with their name. Or find five plain words of your own. If you don't pray, hold their name in five slow breaths, one word of good wishing per breath. Then let the silence do the rest. The bell holds the time.
Beha'alotcha, the portion that ends with Moses' five-word prayer, and a whole people waiting for Miriam.
Your line: short prayers count. Today, when you think of someone hurting, don't wait for the right speech. A name and a few words are enough. Day four hundred forty-five.

446.title: Shelach: go and see (Numbers 13:1–2)
446.hook: twelve scouts are sent to see the land
446.howItsDone: Shelach is read in synagogue in the yearly Torah cycle; the image of two scouts carrying a giant grape cluster on a pole is a familiar one in Jewish art, and the story of the scouts is studied as a lesson in how people see and report.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five words for Miriam, and your line, short prayers count. Did someone hurting get a name and a few words from you? Today a new portion, and the people are at the edge of the land. Day four hundred forty-six.

Before you sign a lease, you visit the apartment. You open the closets, run the shower, check whether the windows face a brick wall. Before a big move, people drive through the new town at night to see if it's quiet. Nobody wants to commit to a place sight unseen. The Israelites are camped in the wilderness of Paran, at the edge of the promised land. The next step is to walk in. And first, someone wants a look around. Today's portion begins with two words, and a story that takes the rest of this week to tell.
screen: `VISIT BEFORE YOU SIGN.` → `AT THE EDGE OF THE LAND.` → `FIRST, A LOOK AROUND.`

segments.voice: God says to Moses: "Send thou men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan". In Hebrew, shelach lecha: send for yourself. That extra word, lecha, for yourself, caught Rashi's eye. He reads it as permission, not command: send, if you want to; I'm not ordering it. Why would God put it that way? Because, in Deuteronomy, Moses remembers that the people asked for it. They wanted a report first. So twelve men go, one leader from each tribe. One of them, Hoshea, gets a new name from Moses: Yehoshua, Joshua. Then Moses gives them a list of questions, and it's a careful list. See the land, what it is. The people living there: strong or weak, few or many. The cities: open camps or fortified. The soil: rich or poor. Are there trees? And be of good courage, he says, and bring back some of its fruit. It was the season of the first ripe grapes. They go for forty days, from the south to the far north. Past Hebron, in a valley later called Eshcol, cluster, they cut a single bunch of grapes so heavy that two men carry it between them on a pole. Pomegranates and figs too. Looking isn't the problem. Moses asked them to see, and to bring back something real. The verb for their mission, latur, means to scout, to explore, to go around and look. Seeing for yourself is a good instinct. What you do with what you saw, as we'll find, is the test.
screen: `SHELACH LECHA: SEND FOR YOURSELF.` · `TWELVE SCOUTS, ONE PER TRIBE.` · `MOSES' LIST: SEE WHAT IT IS.` · `A CLUSTER CARRIED BY TWO.` · then, large: `GO AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go and look for yourself. Breathe, and think of one thing you've formed an opinion about secondhand: a neighborhood, a coworker, a restaurant, a group of people, a book you've only heard about. Notice where the opinion came from. A review? A rumor? Then picture going to see: walking down that street, having that coffee, reading that first chapter. Then ask Moses' first question: what is it, really? The bell holds the time.
Shelach. Send: the portion where twelve scouts go to see the land, and bring back a cluster of grapes too big for one man.
Your line: go and see. Today, check one secondhand opinion with your own eyes, and bring back something real. Day four hundred forty-six.

447.title: Shelach: as grasshoppers (Numbers 13:33)
447.hook: "we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight"
447.howItsDone: Teachers often take up the scouts' line about grasshoppers when Shelach is read; they use it, and the midrash on it, to talk about self-image, and about the difference between what we see and what we assume.

segments.voice: Yesterday the scouts went out, and your line was go and see. Did you check one secondhand opinion with your own eyes? Today they come back. Day four hundred forty-seven.

A candidate sits in the hallway before a job interview, already sure he's the least qualified person in the building. When he's called in, his shoulders drop. He talks too fast. He apologizes before answering. And the person across the desk, who had no opinion of him a minute ago, starts to form one, based on the one he walked in with. It isn't magic. People read how we hold ourselves. Twelve scouts come back from forty days in the land, carrying grapes, and ten of them deliver a report with a line in it that people still quote.
screen: `SURE HE'S THE LEAST.` → `PEOPLE READ HOW WE HOLD OURSELVES.` → `TEN SCOUTS, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: The report starts out true. The land does flow with milk and honey, they say, and here's its fruit. Then comes the word but. The people there are strong. The cities are walled and very large. And as the crowd grows uneasy, the report darkens. Ten of the scouts now say the land devours its inhabitants, and everyone there is huge. Then the line: there we saw the Nephilim, the giants, "and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight." Two halves. The first is honest: we felt tiny. The second is a guess dressed up as a fact: so they saw us that way too. How could the scouts possibly know what the people of the land thought of them? A midrash imagines God catching exactly this. I don't mind that you felt like grasshoppers, God says. But who told you how I made you look in their eyes? The Talmud gives the scouts a little evidence: they overheard the locals say there are ants in the vineyards that look like people. But the book of Joshua, later on, tells a different story. A woman in Jericho named Rahab tells two new spies that terror of Israel has fallen on her land, ever since they heard how the sea dried up before them. Their hearts melted. The people the scouts feared were afraid too. The scouts saw a fact, big people in walled cities, and then let a feeling write the rest of the report. Their picture of themselves became the picture they gave everyone else.
screen: `MILK AND HONEY, BUT.` · `GRASSHOPPERS IN OUR OWN SIGHT.` · `WHO TOLD YOU HOW THEY SAW YOU?` · `JERICHO WAS AFRAID TOO.` · then, large: `HOW YOU SEE YOURSELF SHOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how you see yourself. Breathe, and think of one situation coming up this week that makes you feel small: a meeting, a family dinner, a phone call, a room full of people who seem bigger. Notice the picture you already have of yourself walking in. Now separate the two halves, the way the verse does. What do you actually feel? And what are you guessing they'll think? Let the guess go, just for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Shelach, the scouts' portion. Today: grasshoppers in our own sight, and the guess that others saw us the same way.
Your line: how you see yourself shows. Today, walk into one room without deciding in advance how small you are there. Day four hundred forty-seven.

448.title: Shelach: another spirit (Numbers 14:24)
448.hook: Caleb "had another spirit with him" and trusted they could go up
448.howItsDone: Caleb and Joshua are remembered in Jewish teaching as the two scouts who trusted; the Talmud's account of Caleb praying alone at the patriarchs' graves in Hebron is often told with this portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday the scouts felt like grasshoppers, and your line was how you see yourself shows. Did you walk into a room without shrinking first? Today, the scout who didn't. Day four hundred forty-eight.

The meeting's going badly. Someone has laid out every reason the plan will fail, and they're good reasons. Heads are nodding. The mood in the room is sliding toward no. And then one person, who saw the same numbers, clears their throat and says: actually, I think we can do this. It's not a comfortable moment. The room turns to look at them, and not all the looks are friendly. In Numbers thirteen, that person is named Caleb. He says it to a crowd that's about to cry all night.
screen: `EVERY REASON IT WILL FAIL.` → `THE ROOM SLIDES TOWARD NO.` → `ONE VOICE: WE CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Caleb, from the tribe of Judah, was one of the twelve scouts. He saw the same walls and the same giants. As the others' report spreads fear, he quiets the people and says: let's go up at once and take it; we can certainly do it. The ten answer: we can't. They're stronger than us. That night the whole people weeps. Then Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes in grief and plead: the land is very, very good. Don't rebel. Don't be afraid of its people; God is with us. The crowd's answer is to reach for stones. Then God speaks about Caleb: "But My servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed Me fully", he will enter the land. In Hebrew, ruach acheret: another spirit, a different spirit. Not different eyes; he saw what they saw. A different spirit about what he saw. The Talmud adds a detail from the scouting trip itself. One verse says they went up into the south and he came to Hebron, singular. Who's he? The rabbis say it was Caleb, alone, going to Hebron to pray at the graves of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, asking to be saved from the scouts' plan. The different spirit, in that telling, came with work and prayer, and a willingness to stand apart from his own group. And it lasts. In the book of Joshua, Caleb, now eighty-five, says he's as strong as the day he scouted, and asks for Hebron, giants and all.
